rv.q: This new pairing works wonderfully but its three-week run swiftly sold out.
The ending, when Oldman stares ahead as the light dwindles on the quietly turning tape spools before him, is magnificent.
It takes a lot of genius and a lot of experience to convey oceans of complexity in a few short words – and Oldman's return to Beckett does just that.
Gary Oldman is vividly engaging in Beckett’s bleak monodrama
He is, to be clear, bloody good in Krapp’s Last Tape.
Still, my colleague Dominic Maxwell was slightly underwhelmed when he saw the piece in York, and I have to admit I came away from this evening in much the same mood.

His performance in Krapp's Last Tape is mesmerising: the role requires the actor to bring so much to the act of a cough, a sigh or eating a banana (or three) and Oldman imbues all actions with huge purpose.

It is an understated performance that requires patience from its audience — much of the time Oldman is chuckling or grunting at something his former self has said; in other moments, he sits in silence.

Running at a snappy (is that the right word?!) 1 hour 15 mins straight through, Royal Court's double bill pairs Samuel Beckett's KRAPP'S LAST TAPE featuring Gary Oldman, together with curtain raiser GODOT'S TO-DO LIST, a new piece penned by Leo Simpe-Asante. Artwork provided by production.

He isn’t either as moving or as desperate as some of his predecessors in the role, adopting a richer voice for the recording and a reedy growl as the older Krapp querulously interjects about the younger man’s foolishness.
A fantastic evening that cements Royal Court's 70th year as one of its strongest ever, and certainly a double feature worth waiting for.

cn.t: Oldman's rare stage return in Beckett's classic draws strong praise for its emotional depth, though some find the rigid staging limits fresh interpretation. The double bill with Simpe-Asante's new work makes for a resonant 70th anniversary event.
